ai.claude: A single number that predicts dangerous capabilities would be useful for coordination, but log-perplexity depends on the test data and tokeniser, so it is not directly comparable across labs; any shared limit would need an agreed benchmark and outside auditing, or it is a pledge each lab measures for itself.
ai.fact: OpenAI's chief scientist Jakub Pachocki published the internal log-perplexity scores the company has used since GPT-3.5 to track raw model capability, saying its new skills in cybersecurity and maths arrived below 0.8 and that an unreleased internal model sits at about 0.73. He expects further transformative capabilities around 0.68 to 0.70 and asked other labs to agree common limits until monitoring tools catch up; Sam Altman called it the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while.

austrian.claude: The incentive problem is real, but air-traffic control is a network where one standard and one operator make sense, and privatised systems (Canada's Nav Canada, the UK's NATS) also had big outages. The fix is accountability for unspent money, which is a governance question, not proof that the market would do it better.
austrian.fact: On 13 November the US government grounded every plane in the country; Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy first blamed old routers and asked Congress for $50 billion, while House Democrats noted that most of the $12.5 billion already approved for the same upgrade had not been spent.

opinion.text: Every failure becomes a reason to ask for more money, and Congress rewards it; public agencies shrink their budgets by solving problems and grow them by creating new ones, the same risk-free logic as central banking.

mainstream.fact: The UK agreed a 'soft reset' with the EU that loosens border checks on imports and makes it easier for young Britons and EU nationals to work across the Channel; the business secretary wrote in the FT that the Brexit the country was given has not worked. top.claude: Markets cheered, but the precedent lasts: a company at the centre of US export policy now owes its leadership to a political call, so every future China decision at Nvidia becomes political too.
top.fact: Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive on Monday, two weeks after he was forced out over his affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. The company's statement said input from senior levels of the US government had reassured the board that his return poses no national-security risk; Trump had posted on Sunday that rehiring Huang would be best for the company and the USA, and Semafor reports he joined the board meeting. The stock had lost about 40% in a month before the decision; the reinstatement added roughly $1 trillion of market value.

opinion.text: The board failed at succession planning and now confirms the 'imperial CEO'; the real signal to corporate America is that the last word on a CEO may rest with the president, not shareholders.

top.fact: US futures pointed to a rebound on Monday after Friday's rout, when the Nasdaq posted its worst week since the pandemic and the S&P 500 entered correction territory; Asian markets slumped first, prompting regulators there to intervene. Anthropic and Nvidia both closed Friday down by double digits, Anthropic to just above its $83 IPO price, and the Nasdaq 100 slipped into a bear market. top.fact: Saudi Arabia said it intercepted a Houthi ballistic missile and drone over the weekend, Bahrain said an Iranian strike on an industrial site injured two people, and two oil tankers were hit near Oman. Iran is reportedly preparing to move 14 vessels recently loaded at Kharg Island in an attempt to break the US naval blockade of its oil exports, while its foreign minister said the June memorandum signed in Versailles is no longer valid but could underpin a future deal. Qatar's prime minister, the chief mediator, meets Secretary of State Rubio in Washington today.

top.claude: Hitting Russian ships in the Mediterranean and the Baltic shows Ukraine can reach Moscow's supply lines far from the front, but it also pulls NATO coastal states such as Finland closer to the fighting.
top.fact: Kyiv sank a Russian warship refuelling off the coast of Libya, a day after a drone set a US-sanctioned Russian military logistics ship ablaze in the Gulf of Finland; Russian crews towed it out of Finnish waters. Russia retaliated with a heavy attack on Ukraine's energy infrastructure and civilian sites, killing at least a dozen people. Finland's prime minister Orpo warned that the war is spilling over, and European LNG prices rose ahead of winter.

top.claude: A shortfall against a pre-pandemic trend is not the same as jobs destroyed by AI: higher interest rates and post-Covid over-hiring also cut white-collar hiring. The strongest signal is the entry-level squeeze, because that is where AI substitutes most directly for routine work.
top.fact: A report by RAISE US, led by a former US commerce secretary, and a labour research group finds 1.5 million fewer white-collar jobs in the US than pre-pandemic trends predicted, and says AI is already making it harder for young people to enter the labour market. Bloomberg reports a double-digit decline in AI-exposed jobs in China. The IMF's managing director last month called the effect a slow-moving tsunami.

top.fact: Mexican forces, supported by the US Department of Homeland Security and other agencies, arrested Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, one of the FBI's ten most-wanted, according to the US attorney general. Violence erupted again in Sinaloa after the capture. Ties had been strained since CIA officials took part in a meth-lab raid in northern Mexico this year, which President Sheinbaum called a violation of sovereignty.

opinion.text: A win-win: Washington gets a bounty target, Sheinbaum shows she is tough on crime and can work with Trump, but removing a kingpin often starts a bloody succession war.
